content.thinking:
I need to figure out the actual symptom here: shoppers' stored monthly spend totals came up short of their real purchases, which means user statements would show incorrect totals. I'm trying to pin down whether this is about the monthly aggregate or the total_cents field specifically.

Building the causal chain, the single traceable change is the monthly-spend-feature flag switching on, since purchases made after that point stopped reconciling with the stored totals. Deploys around that time don't show anything relevant, and there's no other change in the record to implicate, so the flag flip looks like the sole candidate cause.

out total_this_month_cents, while the flag-off path does. I'm tightening the causal chain: the flag flips writes to route through this derive-the-month path (P1, F1), and that path by design skips updating the stored total. The link between the flag and derive_the_month=True is inferred rather than directly shown, since F1 notes nothing in this module itself reads the flag — so I should phrase that step as likely rather than certain.

I'm confirming this reaches a definitive cause, resting only on an unrun reading (F1), with no supporting S or D evidence, and noting the lingering risk that the already-stored month totals remain incorrect even after any fix.

Every purchase processed while the flag remains on would continue to understate the monthly total, meaning any statements, averages, or comparisons reading those values (U1-U3, U6) would be wrong — though I don't see a division-by-zero risk there since denominators come from list lengths. As for the flag's status near the incident, the available history doesn't explicitly show it being reverted, and a later note about restoring the feature was left for someone else, so I'll assume it stayed on through the stop point. Now I'm starting to list contributing factors, beginning with how often the spend-integrity check actually runs.

The check only runs on a slow cadence, meaning the fault went undetected until the alert fired well after onset — if it ran more frequently, or after flag changes, totals would've diverged less before being caught, so I'll propose a detection-related action around reconciliation frequency. I'm also considering whether the lack of paging for this alert counts as a contributing factor; Argus did act quickly on its own, but without paging a human might not have acted on the rollback recommendation as promptly, so I'll frame that as a process/detection gap rather than a root cause.

For the other factors: no test existed for the monthly flag case before it was enabled, which the fix PR now addresses with new tests, so that's covered. And the flag itself was flipped on for all traffic at once with no staged rollout or reconciliation gate — I should propose running a reconciliation check as a gate whenever this flag changes, possibly merging it with the earlier detection-frequency proposal.

I'm also noting action items around the repair script — someone needs to review and run it against an export before loading results back, and the patch should be deployed before the flag is re-enabled. I also need to check whether any shopper-facing statements were already rendered with the bad totals.

For the lessons section, I'm starting with what went well: Argus correctly located the onset and traced it to the flag change, forming a candidate alert event after that trigger.

Code-Fix also drafted a proposed fix with tests and a repair script following the same alert, and Argus appropriately held off from acting without a verification path, which counts as a good outcome since it recommended rather than acting blindly.

For what went wrong, I'm weighing a few candidates—the empty log query window and the fact nobody paged—but these feel more like limitations of the record than actual failures, so I'll likely leave that section empty and move to assessing whether there was any customer loss, which appears to be none.

Drafting the symptom line to stay under sixteen words without numbers: shopper monthly spend totals fell short of the purchases behind them. Then building step one of the chain with the reconciliation count and widest shortfall as placeholders, dropping the "otherwise served normally" claim since error rate wasn't actually measured. Now sketching detection action items, starting with running the spend-integrity check more frequently than the current interval.

The extra prevention item is already covered by AI-1, so I'll skip duplicating it. CF-2 maps to AI-1, CF-3 to the flag rollout process, and CF-4 confirms alert routing was the gap — if routing had included paging, someone would've caught it and reverted the flag sooner. Now I'll write this all up.

action_items.item: Run the spend-integrity check much more often than once every {A5} days.
Page on-call when SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile fires on io-shop.
Make running the spend reconciliation part of switching any io-shop feature flag, and check it soon after the switch.
Before running scripts/repair_monthly_spend_totals.py, confirm that the account export really is JSON lines shaped like `io_shop.accounts.Account`, as Code-Fix assumed.
Once the fix is deployed, run scripts/repair_monthly_spend_totals.py with `--write`, load its corrected accounts back into the store, and do this before switching monthly-spend-feature back on.
Find any monthly statements or spend summaries shown to shoppers while their month totals were short, and correct them.

causal_chain.step: Shoppers' stored spend totals no longer matched the purchases behind them: {A1} of {A2} totals the spend-integrity check looked at did not reconcile, the widest short by {A3}. The oldest affected purchase was recorded at {A4}.

Purchases recorded from the onset on were added to each shopper's purchase history but not to the stored month total, which the reconciliation compares with the sum of the month's purchases. So each total fell behind by the price of every such purchase. This rests on Code-Fix's reading of the code, which nothing ran.

ruled_out.what: A deploy or release in the window before the alert: no deploys came back, and the flag change was the only production change read back.

causal_chain.step: An admin switched the monthly-spend-feature flag on at {P1.1}, shortly before the oldest affected purchase at {A4}. According to Code-Fix's reading, with the feature on, `record_a_purchase` is called with `derive_the_month=True` and hands each purchase to `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` rather than to `record_purchase`.

`record_purchase_deriving_the_month` moves `total_cents` but by design never writes `total_this_month_cents`: its docstring says the purchase is recorded "without the month's total being moved". The flag-off path, `record_purchase`, does add the price to the month total.

input.cause_in_plain_words: Switching on a new feature likely sent shoppers' purchases through a way of recording them that adds each purchase to the shopper's history but not to their running total for the month, so those monthly totals came up short.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-integrity check that found the fault runs only once every {A5} days, and no other check of the stored totals was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A more frequent reconciliation would have caught the short totals much sooner after the flag was switched on, with fewer purchases written short and fewer totals to repair.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: No test was seen that recorded a purchase with `derive_the_month=True` and checked the month total. The cases that do this are new in Code-Fix's proposed patch.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: Such a test would have failed on the code as it stood (Code-Fix expects it to get {F1.3} where it expects {F1.4}), exposing the missing month-total update before the flag was switched on.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

contributing_factors.factor: No check that spend totals still reconciled was seen after monthly-spend-feature was switched on, either before or right after the switch.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A reconciliation run tied to the flag change would have shown the totals going short right after the switch, and the flag could have been put back almost at once.
contributing_factors.label: CF-3

contributing_factors.factor: The SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert is not linked to paging, so no person was paged when it fired.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A person would have been told to act at once on the recommendation to put monthly-spend-feature back, cutting short the stretch in which new purchases keep the totals short.
contributing_factors.label: CF-4

went_well: Argus tied the alert to the monthly-spend-feature flag change and formed its candidate causes {T12.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.
Argus did not flip the flag itself when nothing could tell it within its wait whether the action worked. It left putting the flag back to a person as a recommendation.
Code-Fix opened draft pull request #355, with new tests and a one-off repair script, {T19.1 - alert_raised} after the alert was raised.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, purchases are recorded through `record_purchase_deriving_the_month` in src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py. That function adds the purchase to the history and moves `total_cents`, but by design it never writes `total_this_month_cents`, so every purchase recorded that way leaves the stored month total short by that purchase's price. The flag-off path, `record_purchase`, does add the price.
input.still_at_risk: The stored monthly totals were still short, and while monthly-spend-feature stays on, every new purchase is likely to leave them shorter. The monthly statements, spending comparisons and per-item averages that read those totals would show the wrong figures.
input.symptom: Shoppers' monthly spend totals fell short of the purchases behind them
